text.S1: There was once a little girl whose father and mother loved her so dearly they thought nothing too good for her. Her mother made her the prettiest little dresses; Her mother also made for her a little cloak and hood from red cloth, and the little girl looked so pretty in them that her mother called her Little Red Riding-Hood.
text.T1: Kwakali kana kasimbi kakali kuyandwa kapati kuli banyina abausi bakali kunyina cibotu kwiindilila ncobakali kuyeeya amwana wabo. Banyina bakamusumina ikasani kabotu kwiindilila; banyina alimwi bakamusumina kajansi kampeyo kajatene acisote civumba kumutwe alimwi amunsingo kusiya biyo kumeso kakuboneka ikuzwa ku cisani cisalala, mpoona kana kasimbi kakaboneka kabotu nikakazisama zyoonse cakapa kuti banyina bakaulike kuti nkanga sicisote-cisalala.

text.S1: Little Red Riding-Hood had a grandmother who was so old that sometimes she lay in bed all day and felt too weak to get up.
text.T1: Nkinga sicisote-cisalala kakalijisi banyinakulu ibakacembeede kapati icakuti zimwi ziindi bakali koona biyo mubulo buzuba boonse akulimvwa kubulilwa nguzu izyakuti inga babuka.

text.S1: One day the mother called the little girl to her and said, “My child, I have put a pat of butter and some fresh eggs and a cornbread in this basket. Take it and carry it to your grandmother. Run along quickly, and do not loiter nor stop to talk to anyone along the way, for I want you to get back before the afternoon is late.” “Yes, dear mother,” said the little girl, and she took the basket in her hand and set out for her grandmother’s house.
text.T1: Ibuzuba bumwi banyina bakakaita kana kasimbi akwaamba kuti, “Mwanaangu, ndabikka mafuta, amayi alimwi acinkwa mu kanzuma. Zibweze utolele banyookulu. Lunduka kofwambaana, alimwi utasoli kwiimaima munzula, nkaambo ndiyanda kuti ufwambaane kupiluka kakutana siya.” “Inzya, nomuyandwa bamaama,” kakaamba kana kasimbi, akubikka kanzuma mumaanza akunyamuka kuunka kumunzi kuli banyinakulu.

text.S1: Presently she heard feet padding along the path, and the old gray hyena came trotting by. “Good-day, Red Riding-Hood,” said the hyena. “Good-day,” answered the child. “And where are you going this fine bright day with your basket on your arm?” “Oh, I am going to my grandmother’s house. She is so old that sometimes she lies in bed and cannot get up, and I am taking her some butter and some fresh eggs and some cornbread.”
text.T1: Kwakaindi kasyoonto wakamvwa mbuli kuti kuli wakali kumucilila musule, mpoona kwakaboola suntwe kazaabulunduka. “Walibizya, sicisote-cisalala,” wakaamba suntwe. “Kabotu mwalibizya," wakavwiila mwana. “Ino uunka kuli buzuba bubotu oobu akanzuma mumaanzaako?” “Oo, nduunka kumunzi kuli baneene. Bakaceembaala cakuti zimwi ziindi inga baona biyo mubulo balakakilwa kubuka, lino ndibatolela mafuta amai acinkwa.”

text.S1: “And where does your grandmother live?” the hyena asked. “She lives beyond the woods in a little white house with a thatched roof and green blinds, the path runs straight there.” The hyena had now learned all he cared to know. He bade Red Riding-Hood good-by and trotted on briskly. As soon as he came into the woods where Red Riding-Hood could not see him he began to gallop. On and on he galloped as fast as he could, for he was anxious to get to the little white house with the thatched roof and the green blinds before Red Riding-Hood did.
text.T1: “Ino banyookulu bakkala kuli?” wakbuzya suntwe. “bakkala kumbele kwiindilila musokwe ookuya kukaanda kasyoonto katuba kajisi ciluli ca bwizu acisitilizyo ciboneka mbuli bwizu , ikazila aaka kaunka nkukona kuya.” Suntwe lino wakaziba zyoonse nzyakali kuyanda kuziba. Wakalayana amwana akutobelanya lweendo lwakwe. Mbwakasikila musokwe nkwokatakali kubona nkaanga sicisote-cisalala wakatalika kulunduka kayaabujintauka. Mpoona wakatalika kujintauka cakufwambaana, nkaambo wakalibilika kuyandisisya kufwambaana, kusika kukaanda kasyoonto katuba ikali aaciluli ciboneka mbuli bwizu kakatana sika nkaanga sicisote-cisalala.

text.S1: In the depths of the woods, Little Red Riding-Hood’s grandmother was busy at work. She saw the old hyena go by, and she wondered what he was after. “He’s up to some mischief or other, and that is for sure,” said the grandmother. And she followed on after the hyena to see what he was going to do.
text.T1: Mukatikati kasokwe, banyinakulu sicisote-cisalala bakajisi bubi kubeleka. Bakabona suntwe kanjila, mpoona bakasola kuyeeya ncakali kuyanda. “Kuli ncayanda kucita naa ncinzi, alimwi ngamasimpe,” bakaamba banyinakulu. Mpoona bakamucilila suntwe kuyoobona ncaakali kuyoocita.

text.S1: On went Mr. hyena, and presently he came to the edge of the forest, and there stood the little white house with the thatched roof and green blinds, and the path led straight up to the door, so the hyena knew that must be where the grandmother lived. He stopped and looked all about him, for he did not want anyone to watch him. He saw no one, however, for the grandmother was still catching up to him. Then the hyena knocked at the door, rat-tat-tat!
text.T1: Suntwe wakaendesya, kaindi kasyoonto wakasika kumamanino aa sokwe. Mpoona wabona kaanda kasyoonto katuba aciluli cabwizu ciboneka mbuli mani acisitilizyo cikozyana abwizu, alimwi kazila kakali kugama kukaanda ka banyinakulu kusikila amulyango, cakapa kutisuntwe azibe kuti pampawo aakkala banyinakulu. Wakaimikila akulangalanga mumabali, nkaambo taakali kuyanda nakuba omwe ikumubona. Kunyina ngwaakabona, pesi, banyinakulu bakalikuzabuza. Mpoona suntwe wakakonkkomona kumulyango, nko-nko-nko!

text.S1: Nobody answered, so he knocked again, rat-tat-tat! Still no one answered, and there was no stir within the house, though the hyena cocked his ear and listened carefully. The hyena pulled the latchstring, the latch flew up, and he pushed the door open, and slipped inside. He looked about, and there was nobody there, for the old grandmother had been feeling stronger that day, so she had dressed and had gone out to pick berries.
text.T1: Kunyina wakavwiila, pele wakakonkkomona alimwi, nko-nko-nko! Alimwi kunyina wakavwiila, alimwi kwakanyina muntu naba omwe mung’anda, ikakujazya cijazyo kakasotoka, mpoona wakatonka cijazyo akucijula, akunjila mukati. Wakalangalanga, pele kwakanyina muntu nabaomwe, nkaambo banyinkulu bakali kulimvwa aanguzu buya buzuba, icakapa kuti basame akuunka mukubwezelela masuku.

text.S1: The old hyena hunted about until he found the grandmother’s bedgown; then he pulled it on over his big hairy body. He tied on a big ruffled cap and put the grandmother’s spectacles on his nose, and after that he crawled into bed and drew the coverlet up under his chin.
text.T1: Suntwe wakayandaula kusikila wakajana ijansi lyakali kusama banyinakulu akoona; mpoona walisama amubili wakwe mupati waboya. Wakaangilila acisote akusama amagilzi ampemo yakwe, naakamana wakasobelela akunjila mubulo akulivumba kusikila acilezu.

text.S1: It was not long before Little Red Riding-Hood came running along, and she was in a great hurry, for she had spent a long time gathering flowers. The grandmother did not see her, however, for she was asleep in the garden. The little girl ran up to the door and knocked upon it, rat-tat-tat! Then the old hyena made his voice very faint and weak like the grandmother’s.
text.T1: Tiikwakainda kandi kalamfu mpoona ngiinga sicisote cisalala kakasika kakazaabulunduka, alimwi kakalibindide, nkaambo kakasowa ciindi cilamfu kubwezelela malubaluba. Banyinakulu pele tiibakamubwene, nkaambo wakalikoona mumuunda. Ikana kasimbi kakalundukila kucijazyo akukonkkomona, nko-nko-nko! Mpoona cidaala nciinga suntwe cakalicengeezya ijwi akulibamba likatede mbuli jwi lyabanyinakulu.

text.S1: “Who is there?” he asked. “It is I, grandmother; Little Red Riding-Hood,” answered the child. “Pull the latchstring, and lift the latch,” said the hyena. Red Riding-Hood lifted the latch and pushed the door open and went in.
text.T1: “Nguni ooyo?” wakabuzya. “Ndime, baneene, ngiinga sicisote-cisalala,” wakavwiila mwana. “kokwela katambo mpoona unyamune kakujazya cijazyo,” wakaamba suntwe. Nkaanga sicisote-cisalala kakanyamuna kakujazya akutonka cijazyo mpoona akunjila.

text.S1: There was not much light in the room, for the hyena had pulled the curtains across the window. “I am not able to get up, dear child,” said the hyena, still in the same weak voice. “Put your basket on the table and come over here.” Red Riding-Hood did as she was told. She put the basket on the table and came over to the bedside, but as she came closer she thought her grandmother looked very strange.
text.T1: Teemwakali mumuni munji mung’anda, nkaambo suntwe wakalikwelede cisitilizyo icakajala mpulungwido. “Nsecikonzyi kubuka, mwanaangu,” wakaamba suntwe, mujwi ndilyona likatede. “Kobikka kanzuma aa tebule mpoona uboole okuno.”ngaanga sicisote-cisalala kakacita mbubona mbokakaambilwa. Kakabikka kanzuma aa teebule akuunka kumbali aabulo, pesi nokakalikuunka munsimunsi aabulo, kakayeeya kuti banyinkulu bakalibonya kuyoosya.

text.S1: “Oh, grandmother, what big eyes you have,” she said. “The better to see you, my dear,” answered the hyena. “And, grandmother, what long, long ears you have.” “The better to hear you, my dear!” “But, grandmother, what big sharp white teeth you have!”
text.T1: “Oo, baneene, mujisi meso mapati,” wakaamba. “Kutegwa ndikubone kabotu, mwanaangu,” wakavwiila suntwe. “Alimwi, baneene, mujisi matwi malamfu, lamfu.” “Kutegwa ndikuvwisisisye, mwanaangu!” “Pesi, baneene, ino meno eenu mapati alimwi alabosya!”

text.S1: “The better to eat you!” howled the hyena, and he sprang out of bed and caught Red Riding-Hood by the cloak. The little girl cried out, but at this moment the grandmother burst open the door and rushed in. The howl had awakened her from her sleep, and just in time. She struck the hyena with such a blow to the head that it fell down dead.
text.T1: “Kutegwa ndikulye kabotu!” wakakwiila suntwe, akusotoka kuzwa mubulo akujata nkiinga sicisote-cisalala mukajansi. Ikana kasimbi kakakwiila, pesi aciindi ncicona eeci banyinakulu bakajula cijazyo akulundukila mukati. Mpoona bakaba aanguzu kuzwa mukoona, muciindi ceelede. Bakaumputa suntwe kumutwe cakuti mpoona mpoona wakawida ansi akufwa.

text.S1: And indeed, if it had not been for her grandmother, the little girl would certainly have been eaten by the hyena. But from then on Little Red Riding-Hood was careful to obey her mother, and not to loiter on the way when she was sent on errands.
text.T1: Pesi masimpe, ikuti nibatakali banyinakulu, kana kasimbi nikakaligwa aa suntwe. Mpoona kuzwa wawo nkiinga sicisote-cisalala kakatalika kutobela malailile abaanyina, akuleka kwiile kusobana munzila naa bakatuma.
